summary:
The Tacna region stands under Peru's national framework. Peru does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity, which has been lawful since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to rape. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity itself is not an offence.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage. The repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, following an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures. Investigators may still label a killing a hate crime, but that label carries no separate legal consequence; anti-trans violence is prosecuted as ordinary homicide.

Legal recognition of gender is partial. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity, but no gender-identity-recognition statute is in force. The Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents in 2014, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to identity documents was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Access to public facilities matching gender identity is restricted by law. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, and also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The underlying bills, 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, were presented by legislators including Jorge Montoya and Muñante of Honor y Democracia, and the committee approved the dictamen unanimously for plenary on 20 February 2025. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru finds the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their identity, implicitly casting trans people as harassment risks; it invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

A trans woman was killed in Tacna in April 2025. Marcia Paucara Cora, 48, was found dead in a hostel room in central Tacna on 19 April 2025; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel, the Los 5 Titos on Arias y Aragüez street, with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone about two hours later carrying a white bag. She was initially processed as an unidentified body and identified through the hostel's cameras. Police analysed surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the escape route, and as of 21 May 2025 no suspect had been identified. Her family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. The Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021, of which 55.8% of victims were gay men and 36.4% trans women.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. A July 2024 report finds hate crimes increasing in Peru with trans women most affected, and co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
tangentialFactors:
Tacna is a border city with heavy transit, and the hostel in the Paucara Cora case was in the central district, the kind of short-stay accommodation where a visitor is registered under whatever identity is given at the desk. The man who accompanied her used a false identity and was not traced; visitors should expect that a complaint filed in such premises depends on camera coverage and staff cooperation rather than on any anti-discrimination duty.

Peru's position on LGBT protection is an outlier in its subregion. The country is one of only three South American states, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, and the 2017 repeal of Decree Nº 1323's Articles 46 and 323 was a legislative act rather than a judicial one, carried after a Constitutional Committee vote and a petition claiming one million signatures. Comparatively, the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, which IDEHPUCP invokes against the restroom ban, binds the wider Inter-American system and gives a visitor a documented external standard to cite, even though Peru's own legislature has moved in the opposite direction with Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 and the April 2025 sexual-integrity law.

The trajectory of hostile measures is worth tracking for anyone transiting the country across a longer period. Restroom restrictions and the biological-sex rule were adopted in April and May 2025, while the Azul Rojas Marín judgment of 15 December 2025 shows litigation can still produce accountability after decades. Both directions of movement are live, and neither settles what a trans visitor will encounter at a hotel desk, a police station, or a clinic.
localsOnly:
Residents can change their legal name to match their gender identity, and since the Constitutional Court's ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November they can change the gender marker on national identity documents through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery, reversing the Court's own 2014 prohibition. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications shifted twice in 2024. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Economic exposure is documented. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, an exposure factor that the recorded violence figures reflect: the Public Prosecutor's Office logged 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021, with trans women accounting for 36.4% of victims.

Organising carries new risk. An April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, and Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional, showing that judicial remedies remain available.
